(i) Solid: C20H41OH is a large molecule with strong London (van der Waals) forces between the long chains, plus hydrogen bonding from –OH. You must discuss the intermolecular forces; “high Mr” alone is not enough.

(ii) The long non-polar hydrocarbon chain (many C–C and C–H bonds) outweighs the single polar –OH group, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water to any great extent and is only slightly soluble.

BF3: only three electron pairs (all bonding) around B, which repel to 120° → trigonal planar.

NF3: four electron pairs around N (three bonding + one lone pair) → tetrahedral electron domain, so the molecular shape is trigonal pyramidal. (Explanation via sp2/sp3 also accepted.)

BrF5: six electron domains around Br (five bonding pairs + one lone pair) → octahedral electron domain geometry, molecular shape square pyramidal.

Diagram: Br in the centre, four F in a square plane, one F above, lone pair pointing down (lone pair shown if you call it “octahedral-based”).

C2H2 (ethyne) has a triple bond: one σ bond (sp–sp overlap) and two π bonds.

“Triple bond” alone earns only 1 mark.

(These are Q8(c) on the paper.)

(i) Butane is non-polar, so only weak London (dispersion/van der Waals) forces act between molecules → lowest b.p.

(ii) Propan-1-ol has H bonded directly to the very electronegative O atom, so strong hydrogen bonds form between molecules → highest b.p.

(iii) O is more electronegative than C, so the C=O bond is polar: dipole–dipole attractions (plus London forces) between propanal molecules.

(Q8(e) on the paper.) Evidence (any three): all C–C bond lengths equal (between single and double); all C–C bond enthalpies equal; benzene does not readily undergo addition reactions; only one isomer of 1,2-disubstituted benzene exists; enthalpy of hydrogenation (or combustion) is less exothermic than expected for three C=C bonds; 1H NMR shows a single peak at a shift unlike an alkene.

Bonding: each C is sp2 hybridised, forming σ bonds in a planar hexagon; the six unhybridised p electrons (one per C) overlap to form a delocalised π system above and below the ring.

Explanations: delocalisation gives extra stability (≈150 kJ mol−1), so addition (which destroys the π system) is unfavourable and ΔH of hydrogenation is less negative than predicted; every C–C bond is identical (intermediate between single and double), so all lengths/strengths are equal and there cannot be two 1,2-isomers.
C3H8 has the higher boiling point: it has a larger Mr (more electrons), so its London (dispersion) forces are stronger and more energy is needed to separate the molecules.

CH3CH2OH has the higher boiling point: ethanol has an O–H group so hydrogen bonding occurs between its molecules, whereas CH3OCH3 (no H on O) has only dipole–dipole and London forces. More energy is needed to separate ethanol molecules.

The two have the same Mr (46), so the difference is due only to the type of intermolecular force.

(i) N2: :N≡N: (triple bond, one lone pair on each N). NH3: three N–H bonds + one lone pair on N. H2NNH2: N–N single bond, each N with two H and one lone pair. HNNH: H–N=N–H, each N with one lone pair. (Lone pairs must be shown.)

(ii) The H–N–N angles in HNNH (≈120°) are larger than in H2NNH2. In HNNH each N has three electron domains (double bond, N–H bond, lone pair) → trigonal planar arrangement; in H2NNH2 each N has four domains → tetrahedral, with angles slightly less than 109.5° (≈107°) due to the lone pair.

(iii) N2: sp; NH3: sp3; HNNH: sp2.

(iv) HNNH has cis/trans (E/Z) isomers because rotation about N=N is restricted. Trans (H atoms on opposite sides) is non-polar — dipoles cancel; cis (H atoms same side) is polar.

(i) H–C(=O)–O–H: 4 σ bonds and 1 π bond. A σ bond is formed by head-on overlap with electron density directly between the nuclei (stronger); a π bond by sideways overlap of p orbitals, with electron density above and below the internuclear axis (weaker).

(ii) The two C–O bonds differ: C=O is shorter than C–O, because the extra shared electron pair pulls the atoms closer.

(iii) In HCOO− both C–O bonds are the same length (intermediate between single and double) because of delocalisation (resonance).

(iv) Two resonance structures: H–C(=O)–O− and −O–C(=O)–H, i.e. the double bond on either oxygen, with all lone pairs on O shown. The real ion is a resonance hybrid: the π electrons are delocalised over both C–O bonds, giving bond order 1½.

(i) A, C and D (boiling points below room temperature, ≈298 K). All three needed.

(ii) A (very low m.p./b.p. and insoluble in water → non-polar).

(iii) London (dispersion / van der Waals / induced dipole–induced dipole) forces — not dipole–dipole.

(iv) Nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine (H bonded to N, O or F).

(v) F, because it has the highest melting and boiling points (many strong covalent bonds must be broken). Explanation required.

(vi) E: a metal (conducts as solid and liquid; reacts with steam). F: a metalloid / semiconductor (e.g. silicon).

(i) Diagram: two CH3COOH molecules joined in a ring by two hydrogen bonds, C=Oδ−···Hδ+–O. In non-polar benzene ethanoic acid exists as this dimer (Mr 120); in water the acid molecules hydrogen bond to water instead, so it exists as monomers (Mr 60). Must mention the non-polar solvent.

(ii) Diagram: in the cis isomer the two –COOH groups are close, so an intramolecular hydrogen bond forms between them. This reduces hydrogen bonding between molecules, so the cis isomer has a lower m.p.; the trans isomer forms more intermolecular hydrogen bonds.

(iii) Diagram: C2H5–Oδ−(H)···Hδ+–O–C2H5. Ethanol forms hydrogen bonds because H is bonded to O; in CH3OCH3 all H atoms are bonded to C, so there is no hydrogen bonding and its b.p. is much lower.

Pt in the centre bonded to two Cl atoms and two NH3 groups (through N), e.g. a square planar Pt with Cl, Cl, NH3, NH3 at the corners. The N atoms bond to Pt by dative (coordination) bonds from their lone pairs.

C2H2: H–C≡C–H (triple bond, no lone pairs on C). Linear, 180°.

C2Cl4: Cl2C=CCl2, each Cl with 3 lone pairs. Each C has 3 electron domains → trigonal planar, 120°.

SF4: S with 4 S–F bonds and one lone pair (expanded octet, 5 domains, each F with 3 lone pairs). Electron domain geometry trigonal bipyramidal; molecular shape see-saw; angles ≈ 90° and 120° (slightly less, due to lone-pair repulsion).

C2H2: sp (2 electron domains per C).

C2Cl4: sp² (3 electron domains per C).

Ethanoate: CH3–C(=O)–O⁻ ↔ CH3–C(–O⁻)=O (the double bond and negative charge swap between the two O atoms). A delocalized structure with a dashed bond and ½− on each O also earns credit.

Benzene: the two Kekulé structures, hexagons with alternating double bonds in the two different positions (or a hexagon with a circle for delocalization).

(i) In ethanoic acid the two C–O bonds are different: C=O is shorter than C–O. In the ethanoate ion both C–O bonds are equal, with an intermediate length (bond order 1.5) because of delocalization (resonance).

(ii) Benzene is stabilized by its delocalized π electrons; addition would destroy the delocalization (lose this stability), so substitution, which keeps the ring intact, is preferred.

(iii) Lower pKa means stronger acid, so ethanoic acid (4.76) is a much stronger acid than ethanol (~16). The ethanoate ion is more stable than the ethoxide ion because its negative charge is delocalized over two O atoms (and the C=O is electron-withdrawing); in ethoxide the charge is localized on one O.

(i) BF3: B with three B–F bonds and no lone pair (only 6 electrons around B). NF3: N with three N–F bonds and one lone pair. BF4⁻: B with four B–F bonds, charge −1. Each F shows 3 lone pairs.

(ii) BF3 trigonal planar (120°); NF3 trigonal pyramidal; BF4⁻ tetrahedral (109.5°). The angle in NF3 (~107°) is smaller than in BF4⁻ because the lone pair on N repels more strongly than bonding pairs, pushing the bonds closer together.

(iii) Hybridization = mixing of atomic orbitals to form new, equivalent hybrid orbitals. BF3: sp²; NF3: sp³.

(iv) A polar bond has an unequal sharing of the bonding electrons; the more electronegative atom has greater electron density (δ−). B–F and N–F are both polar (F is more electronegative). BF3 is non-polar: its symmetrical trigonal planar shape makes the bond dipoles cancel. NF3 is polar: its pyramidal shape means the dipoles do not cancel.

(i) σ bond: end-on (axial) overlap of orbitals along the line between the nuclei. π bond: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, above and below the axis. A double bond = 1σ + 1π; a triple bond = 1σ + 2π.

(ii) Delocalization: bonding electrons that are not confined to two atoms but are spread over three or more atoms.

(iii) Enthalpy diagram: three reactant levels above pentane, drops of 126 (1), 254 (2) and 226 (3) kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH2 ≈ 2ΔH1 because twice as many C=C and H–H bonds are broken and C–H/C–C formed. Molecule 3 has conjugated double bonds (alternating), allowing delocalization of π electrons, which stabilizes it, so less energy is released (−226 rather than ≈ −252).

Increasing boiling point: B < A < C.

  • B (butanal): only dipole–dipole (and London) forces; no hydrogen bonding.
  • A (butan-1-ol): hydrogen bonding between molecules.
  • C (butanoic acid): more/stronger hydrogen bonding (two O atoms; forms dimers), so highest.

(i) Diamond: a giant covalent network, each C bonded to four others, so atoms are held strongly in place → very hard; all outer electrons are used in localized bonds → no mobile electrons → does not conduct. Graphite: layers of C atoms (each bonded to three others) held together by weak London forces, so layers slide → soft; each C has one delocalized electron free to move along the layers → conducts.

(ii) Within F2: a single covalent bond (shared pair). Between molecules: weak London (dispersion) forces between temporary dipoles.

(iii) In the solid, ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move; when molten the ions are free to move and carry charge.

(i) XeF4: 4 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs (6 domains, octahedral arrangement) → square planar.

(ii) NH4⁺: 4 bonding pairs → tetrahedral (109.5°).

(iii) PCl6⁻: 6 bonding pairs → octahedral (90°).

(i) Hybridization: mixing of atomic orbitals (s and p) to form new, equivalent hybrid orbitals with character of both. σ bond: end-on (head-on) overlap of orbitals, with electron density concentrated between the nuclei. In ethane each C is sp³ hybridized (four σ bonds).

(ii) π bond: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, with electron density above and below the internuclear axis. Ethene: sp²; ethyne: sp.

• BF4⁻: B with four single bonds to F (each F with 3 lone pairs), charge −1.
  • H2CO: C bonded to two H and double-bonded to O (O with 2 lone pairs).
  • NO2⁺: [O=N=O]⁺, each O with 2 lone pairs, no lone pair on N.
  • NO2⁻: one N=O and one N–O⁻, with one lone pair on N (O atoms with 2 and 3 lone pairs).

All valence electrons and the ion charges must be shown.

• BF4⁻: 4 bonding domains, equal repulsion → tetrahedral, 109.5°.
  • H2CO: 3 domains → trigonal planar, ~120°.
  • NO2⁺: 2 domains → linear, 180°.
  • NO2⁻: 3 domains (2 bonding + 1 lone pair) → bent/V-shaped, ~115° (less than 120°), because the lone pair repels more than bonding pairs.

Hybridization: the mixing of atomic orbitals to form new, equivalent hybrid orbitals.

BF4⁻ sp³; H2CO sp²; NO2⁺ sp; NO2⁻ sp².

Both are covalent bonds (shared electron pairs).

  • C–O single bond: a σ bond only, formed by end-on (axial) overlap of orbitals.
  • C=O double bond: one σ bond + one π bond; the π bond forms by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals.

The C=O bond is shorter and stronger than the C–O bond (more shared electrons pull the nuclei closer).

(i) The π electrons are delocalized over the C and both O atoms, so the two C–O bonds are identical (equal length, bond order 1.5) – a resonance hybrid.

(ii) Between C=O (0.122 nm) and C–O (0.143 nm): about 0.128–0.136 nm.

H2S → H2Se → H2Te: molecules get larger (more electrons), so London (van der Waals') forces increase and b.p. rises [1].

H2O is anomalously high because it forms hydrogen bonds (H bonded to the very electronegative, small O with lone pairs) [1]; hydrogen bonds are much stronger than the London forces in the others [1].

(i) Insoluble: butane — non-polar, only London forces, cannot interact with/disrupt water's H-bonds [1]; chloroethane — only slightly polar, cannot hydrogen bond with water [1].

(ii) Soluble: propanone — polar C=O whose O lone pairs accept H-bonds from water [1]; propan-1-ol — O–H group forms hydrogen bonds with water [1].

(i) CO: :C≡O: (triple bond, one lone pair on each atom). CO2: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O. CO32−: C with one C=O and two C–O−, all O completing octets, charge 2− shown (bracket/charge needed). [1] each.

(ii) CO32− [1]: resonance gives each C–O a bond order of 1⅓, compared with 2 in CO2 and 3 in CO [1]; fewer shared electrons hold the nuclei less tightly, so the bond is longer [1].

(iii) ClF3: Cl with three Cl–F bonds and two lone pairs; each F has three lone pairs [1]. Five electron domains (trigonal bipyramidal), lone pairs equatorial → T-shaped [1].

(i) I: N=N=N–H with appropriate lone pairs (central N no lone pair; H-bearing N one lone pair). II: N≡N–N–H with the H-bearing N having two lone pairs (formal charges not required). [1] each.

(ii) N–N–N = 180° in both: central N has two electron domains, which repel to be as far apart as possible [2].
I: H–N–N ≈ 120° (slightly less): three electron domains (one a lone pair) [2].
II: H–N–N ≈ 104–109°: four electron domains, two of them lone pairs; extra lone-pair repulsion compresses the angle [2].

(iii) I: sp2; II: sp3 [1 each].

NO2−: O=N–O− with one lone pair on N (O atoms complete octets); charge shown. NO2+: O=N=O with no lone pair on N, two lone pairs on each O; charge shown.

NO2−: bent/angular (~115–120°) — three electron domains around N, one of which is a lone pair.

NO2+: linear (180°) — two electron domains, no lone pairs on N, repel as far apart as possible.

(i) C2H6 < CH3CHO < C2H5OH < CH3COOH

(ii) C2H6 non-polar; CH3CHO, C2H5OH and CH3COOH polar.
Boiling point depends on the strength of intermolecular forces that must be overcome.
C2H6: London (van der Waals') forces only — weakest.
CH3CHO: dipole–dipole forces (polar C=O) as well.
C2H5OH and CH3COOH: hydrogen bonding (O–H) — strongest.
CH3COOH is highest: more extensive H-bonding (two O atoms, dimers), greater polarity and larger mass/London forces.

(i) Diamond: non-conductor — each C uses all four electrons in localised covalent bonds, so no free electrons. Graphite: good conductor — each C bonds to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that can move between/along the layers.

(ii) KCl conducts only when molten or in aqueous solution, because then its ions are free to move and carry charge (in the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice).

Expected answer: not (very) water soluble, because the ester has no O–H group so cannot hydrogen bond like an alcohol or acid. Also accepted: soluble, because it is a small polar molecule (its O atoms can accept H-bonds from water).

(i) σ bond: head-on (end-to-end) overlap of orbitals [1], with electron density concentrated along the axis between the two nuclei [1].

(ii) π bond: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals [1], with electron density above and below the internuclear axis [1].

(iii) Double bond = 1 σ + 1 π.

(iv) Triple bond = 1 σ + 2 π.

(i) OF2: sp3; bent/V-shaped (~104°): four electron domains on O — 2 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs.

(ii) H2CO: sp2; trigonal planar (~120°): three electron domains on C (two C–H, one C=O).

(iii) C2H2: sp; linear (180°): two electron domains on each C (C–H and C≡C).

(i) Diamond: giant covalent (macromolecular) 3-D network, each C covalently bonded to 4 others (tetrahedral). Graphite: layers of hexagonal rings, each C bonded to 3 others; covalent within layers, weak London forces between layers.

(ii) Diamond: non-conductor (no delocalised electrons); very hard (rigid 3-D network of strong bonds). Graphite: good conductor (one delocalised electron per C); soft/slippery (layers slide over each other).

(iii) C60 is a molecular solid: softer than diamond (and harder than graphite in the markscheme), as only weak intermolecular forces hold the C60 molecules together so they can move over each other. It conducts better than diamond but worse than graphite: some delocalised electrons, but electrons cannot move easily from one molecule to the next.

Any three:

  • count the electron pairs/domains around the central atom;
  • electron domains repel each other;
  • and arrange themselves as far apart as possible (minimum repulsion);
  • a double/triple bond counts as one domain;
  • lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs.

Do not accept repulsion between bonds or atoms.

(i) PCl3: P with three P–Cl bonds and one lone pair. PCl5: P with five P–Cl bonds, no lone pair (expanded octet). POCl3: P=O plus three P–Cl, no lone pair on P. Every Cl carries 3 lone pairs; O carries 2 (in P=O).

(ii)

  • PCl3: trigonal pyramidal, ~100–107° (4 domains, 1 lone pair)
  • PCl5: trigonal bipyramidal, 90° and 120°
  • POCl3: tetrahedral, ~109° (accept 100–112°)

(iii) PCl3 polar – bond dipoles don’t cancel (asymmetric); PCl5 non-polar – symmetric, dipoles cancel; POCl3 polar – P=O and P–Cl dipoles differ so don’t cancel.

(i) Hybridization = mixing of atomic orbitals to form new (hybrid) orbitals of equal energy.

(ii) Propene, CH3CH=CH2:

  • σ bonds: end-on (axial) overlap of orbitals between nuclei – all C–H, C–C, and one of the C=C bonds (8 σ in total);
  • π bond: sideways overlap of p orbitals above and below the bond axis (1 π, in C=C);
  • C–C single bond is longer and weaker than the C=C double bond;
  • CH3 carbon is sp3; the two C=C carbons are sp2.

SiO2 is a giant covalent (macromolecular) network; melting requires breaking many strong Si–O covalent bonds, which needs a lot of energy.

Max [1] without mention of covalent; "broken", not "weakened".
C4H9OH has the higher b.p.: its molecules form hydrogen bonds (O–H), whereas C4H9Br has only weaker London/dipole–dipole forces.

(i) The stronger the intermolecular forces, the greater the enthalpy of vaporization. Pentane has only London (dispersion) forces (27 kJ mol−1); propanoic acid also has hydrogen bonding (57 kJ mol−1).

(ii) Graph: vapour pressure rises with temperature, curving upwards (increasingly steep). As temperature rises, more molecules have enough kinetic energy to overcome the intermolecular forces and escape into the vapour.
p2.flag: (ii) vapour pressure is not explicitly in the 2025 syllabus

p2.key:
• XeF4: Xe with four Xe–F bonds and two lone pairs on Xe;
  • PF5: P with five P–F bonds, no lone pairs;
  • BF4−: B with four B–F bonds, in square brackets with a 1− charge.

Each F has three lone pairs (missing F lone pairs penalized once).

• XeF4: 6 domains (4 bonding, 2 lone pairs opposite each other) → square planar, 90°;
  • PF5: 5 bonding domains → trigonal bipyramidal, 90° and 120°;
  • BF4−: 4 bonding domains → tetrahedral, 109.5°.

Domains repel to positions of minimum repulsion.

Hybridization: mixing of atomic orbitals to form new, equivalent hybrid orbitals.

  • N2 (N≡N): sp
  • N2H2 (HN=NH): sp2
  • N2H4 (H2N–NH2): sp3

• σ bonds form by end-on (axial) overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis;
  • π bonds form by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, above and below the axis;
  • single bonds (N–H) are σ only;
  • the double bond (N=N) is one σ + one π bond.

(i) H2N–CH2–CH2–CH2–CH2–CH2–CH2–NH2 (hexane-1,6-diamine), with a lone pair drawn on each N. Branched chains are accepted if both ends are NH2; no lone pairs = no mark.

(ii) C–N–H ≈ 107° (accept 105–108°). N has three bonding pairs and one lone pair; the lone pair repels the bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other, squeezing the angle below the tetrahedral 109.5° found at C (C–C–N, four bonding pairs).
Hybridization is the mixing of atomic orbitals (e.g. s and p) on an atom to form new hybrid orbitals of equal energy.
The C atom is sp hybridized (two electron domains, linear). The C≡N triple bond has one σ and two π bonds. The sp mark is lost if sp2 or sp3 is also given.

• σ bond: end-on (axial) overlap of orbitals, with the electron density concentrated between the two nuclei, along the internuclear axis.
  • π bond: sideways (parallel) overlap of p orbitals, with the electron density above and below the σ bond (the internuclear axis).

You must mention electrons/electron density to get the 2nd and 4th marks. A labelled diagram can score.

A Kekulé benzene with three C=C bonds would be expected to give 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol−1.

The real value is only −208, so benzene is about 150 kJ mol−1 more stable than a structure with three separate double bonds, because its π electrons are delocalized. Saying “delocalized bonds” is not accepted.

(i) CH3CH2OCH2CH3 (the ether) has the lowest boiling point. It is the only one that cannot hydrogen bond between its molecules (it has only dipole–dipole and London forces).

(ii) T = 70 + 273 = 343 K. V = nRT/p = 0.0200 × 8.31 × 343 ÷ 1.10 × 105 = 5.18 × 10−4 m3 (0.518 dm3).

(iii) C–O.

(iv) m/z 45: COOH+ (acid), OCH2CH3+ (ether), CH2CH2OH+ (alcohol). Charges must be shown.

(i) PCl5: P with five P–Cl bonds and no lone pair on P (three lone pairs on each Cl). Shape: trigonal bipyramidal; angles 90°, 120°, 180° (two correct angles score [1]).

(ii) SCl2: S with two bonds and two lone pairs. Shape: bent (V-shaped); angle about 100–107° (less than 109.5°, because the lone pairs repel more).

(iii) ICl4−: I with four bonds and two lone pairs (six domains, with the lone pairs opposite each other). Shape: square planar; angle 90°.

Missing lone pairs is penalized once.

A: giant covalent network. Its high melting point (1986 K) is because many strong covalent bonds throughout the structure must be broken. It does not conduct because it has no mobile charged particles (ions or electrons).

B: ionic lattice. Its high melting point (1074 K) comes from strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions throughout the lattice. It conducts only when molten or in solution, because the ions are then free to move; in the solid they are fixed.

(i) Hybridization is the mixing of atomic orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals.

(ii) C60: sp2; diamond: sp3; graphite: sp2.

(iii) In both, each C is bonded to only 3 other C atoms. The fourth electron (in an unhybridized p orbital) is delocalized and can move through the structure.

(i) A σ bond forms by end-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis. A π bond forms by sideways overlap of p orbitals (above and below the axis).

(ii) H2C=C(CH3)CH=CH2 (C5H8) has 4 C–C and 8 C–H σ bonds, giving 12 σ bonds, and two C=C, giving 2 π bonds.

XeF2: 2 bonding pairs and 3 lone pairs on Xe (5 domains, trigonal bipyramidal arrangement, with the lone pairs equatorial). Shape: linear, 180°.

BrF2+: 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs on Br (4 domains, tetrahedral arrangement). Shape: bent (V-shaped), angle less than 109.5° (about 90–105°; actual value 93.5°), because the lone pairs repel more.

The explanation must be in words, not just a drawing.

(i) XeF4: Xe has 4 Xe–F bonds and 2 lone pairs (6 domains), so it is square planar. XeO4: Xe has 4 Xe=O bonds and no lone pairs (4 domains), so it is tetrahedral.

(ii) PF5: 5 bonding pairs and no lone pair, so it is trigonal bipyramidal. IF5: 5 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair (6 domains), so it is square pyramidal.

Show three lone pairs on each F (and two on each O). A missing or extra lone pair on the central atom loses the mark each time.

(i) Each C is sp2 hybridized, with bond angles of 120°. The molecule is planar, a regular hexagon. The unhybridized p orbitals overlap to give a delocalized π system above and below the ring, so all C–C bonds are equal (intermediate between single and double; a resonance hybrid).

(ii) One peak: all six H atoms are in the same chemical environment.

• N has 4 electron domains (3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair). These repel to a tetrahedral arrangement.
  • Only the 3 bonding pairs (atoms) define the shape, so it is trigonal pyramidal.
  • The lone pair repels more strongly than bonding pairs, so the angle is squeezed from 109.5° to 107°.

(i) F2O: 2 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs on O, so the electron domains are tetrahedral. The shape is bent (V-shaped) with an angle of about 103° (95–105° accepted).

(ii) ICl4−: 4 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs on I, so the electron domains are octahedral. The shape is square planar (lone pairs opposite each other) with angles of 90°.

(i) A Lewis structure shows all valence electron pairs, both bonding and lone. For CH2=CHCl, draw the C=C double bond, the C–H and C–Cl single bonds, and 3 lone pairs on Cl.

(ii) A σ bond forms by end-on (head-on) overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis. A π bond forms by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, giving electron density above and below the axis. In chloroethene every bond is σ except the C=C, which is one σ + one π.

(iii) Hybridization is the mixing of atomic orbitals to form new, equivalent hybrid orbitals. Both C atoms are sp2 hybridized.

• The C–Cl bond (0.169 nm) is shorter than a normal C–Cl single bond (0.177 nm).
  • A lone pair on Cl overlaps with the C=C π system and becomes delocalized, giving the C–Cl bond some double-bond character.
  • So the C=C bond loses some double-bond character and is slightly longer than 0.134 nm.
  • Predicted C–C length: between 0.134 and 0.154 nm, e.g. about 0.14 nm.

ethene < chloroethene < bromoethene

  • Ethene is non-polar and has only London (dispersion) forces.
  • Chloroethene and bromoethene are polar, so they also have dipole–dipole attractions.
  • Bromoethene has the largest Mr and the most electrons, so its London forces are strongest and its boiling point is highest.

• Al2Cl6 has covalent bonding and a simple molecular structure.
  • The melting point is low because only weak intermolecular forces have to be overcome.
  • It conducts poorly because there are no ions (or delocalized electrons) to carry charge.

(i) F (butan-2-ol) has the highest boiling point. Its strongest intermolecular force is hydrogen bonding.

(ii) E (2-bromobutane) is the least soluble: it cannot form hydrogen bonds with water. Butan-2-ol and butanone can both H-bond with water molecules.

Any four of:

  • An electron is promoted from 2s to 2p.
  • One 2s and one 2p orbital mix to form two sp hybrid orbitals on each C.
  • These sp orbitals form σ bonds (C–C and C–H) by end-on overlap.
  • The two unhybridized 2p orbitals on each C overlap sideways…
  • …to form two π bonds. So C≡C is 1 σ + 2 π.

• The two C=C carbons are sp2, with bond angles of about 120°.
  • The other four ring carbons are sp3, with angles of about 109.5°.

• Alternating single and double bonds would give two bond lengths, 0.154 nm (C–C) and 0.134 nm (C=C).
  • In fact all six C–C bonds in benzene are the same length (0.139 nm), between the two values. This fits a delocalized ring.

(i) In COO−, the p orbitals on C and both O atoms overlap. This forms a delocalized π system over three atoms, so the negative charge is shared between the two O atoms.

(ii) In benzoic acid (COOH) there are two different C–O lengths: C=O is shorter than C–O. In benzoate (COO−) both C–O bonds are the same length, between C=O and C–O.

SF2: S with two single S–F bonds and 2 lone pairs on S (3 lone pairs on each F); 4 electron domains → bent / V-shaped / angular.

SF4: S with four S–F bonds and 1 lone pair on S (expanded octet, 5 domains) → see-saw / distorted tetrahedral.

SF6: S with six S–F bonds, no lone pairs on S (6 domains) → octahedral.

One mark per Lewis structure (lone pairs on S required; missing F lone pairs penalised once) and one per shape name. No ECF from wrong Lewis structures.

Both are simple molecular. S8 is a larger molecule with more electrons (greater Mr) than P4, so it has stronger London (dispersion) forces between molecules, needing more energy to overcome. ("Larger mass" alone not accepted.)

• Si: giant covalent network (3-D lattice) – many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it.
  • Ar: exists as single atoms held only by very weak London (dispersion) forces. ("Molecular" not accepted for Ar.)

Hydrazine: H2N–NH2 with an N–N single bond, two N–H bonds on each N and one lone pair on each N.

Nitrogen: :N≡N: – a triple bond with one lone pair on each N.

Missing lone pairs penalized once.

(i) The π bond forms by sideways overlap of p orbitals (one unhybridized p orbital on each C), giving electron density above and below the C–C axis. A labelled sketch can earn the marks.

(ii) C(1) is sp3 (four single bonds); C(2) is sp2 (part of the C=C double bond).

(i) H2N–NH2: each N has two N–H bonds, an N–N single bond and one lone pair, so 14 valence electrons are shown in total.

(ii) The angle is less than 109.5° (about 107°; accept 104–109°). There are four electron domains around each N (tetrahedral arrangement), and the lone pair repels more strongly than the bonding pairs, which squeezes the H–N–H angle.

Ethene is non-polar and has only weak London (dispersion) forces. Hydrazine has N–H bonds and lone pairs on N, so it forms strong hydrogen bonds between molecules. More energy is needed to separate hydrazine molecules, so its boiling point is higher. A comparison of strengths is needed for 2 marks.

At 30 °C, vapour pressure: ethoxyethane (≈81 × 103 Pa) > benzene (≈16 × 103 Pa) > water (≈4 × 103 Pa).

Water has strong hydrogen bonds, so the fewest molecules escape. Benzene has only London (dispersion) forces, but these are fairly strong for its large, flat electron cloud. Ethoxyethane has dipole–dipole plus London forces, but they are weaker overall than benzene's.

The weaker the intermolecular forces, the higher the vapour pressure.
A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure (≈101 × 103 Pa). Reading this off the benzene curve gives about 81 °C (accept 80–82 °C).

p2.key:
Compare the three allotropes (3 features = 2 marks):

  • Bonding: all have covalent bonds between C atoms. Graphite (between layers) and C60 (between molecules) also have London forces.
  • Structure: diamond is a 3-D covalent network; graphite is a network of flat layers; C60 is a discrete spherical molecule of hexagons and pentagons.
  • Atoms bonded to each C: diamond 4 (tetrahedral); graphite and C60 3.
  • Bond angles / hybridization: diamond 109.5° (sp3); graphite 120° (sp2); C60 between 109° and 120°.
  • Delocalized electrons: present in graphite and C60, absent in diamond.

(i) SiO2 is a giant covalent (network) structure. Each Si is covalently bonded to 4 O atoms (tetrahedral), and each O is bonded to 2 Si atoms.

(ii) To melt SiO2, many strong covalent bonds in the network must be broken, so it is a solid. CO2 is made of small separate molecules held by weak London forces, which need little energy to overcome, so it is a gas.

There is a triple bond between C and O: two ordinary shared pairs plus one coordinate (dative) bond in which O donates a lone pair to C. Each atom keeps one lone pair: :C≡O:. Drawing only C≡O scores 1 mark.

The π electrons are delocalized over all three C–O bonds (spread over more than two nuclei), instead of sitting in one C=O double bond. As a result, all three C–O bonds have the same length and strength (bond order 1⅓), and the 2− charge is spread evenly over the three O atoms.

Delocalization lowers the energy, so the ion is more stable. You can show three resonance structures or a single delocalized structure with a 2− charge.

Hybridization: the mixing of atomic orbitals to form new, equivalent hybrid orbitals for bonding.

CO2: sp; diamond: sp3; graphite: sp2; carbonate ion: sp2.

Why: the hybridization follows the number of electron domains around C: 2 → sp, 3 → sp2, 4 → sp3.

Methoxymethane has no H bonded to O, so its molecules are held only by weak London and dipole–dipole forces.

Ethanol has an O–H group, so it forms hydrogen bonds between molecules.

Hydrogen bonds are stronger than these other intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate ethanol molecules, and its boiling point is higher. Mentioning covalent bonds breaking on boiling loses a mark.

p2.key:
(i) Sodium reacts violently with any moisture, forming flammable/explosive hydrogen, so it must be removed ("too reactive" alone is not enough).

(ii) Structure: giant network in which each Si is bonded tetrahedrally to 4 O atoms and each O bridges two Si atoms (draw Si with 4 O, extension bonds shown, not 90° angles).
Bonding: giant/network (3D) covalent.

Butan-1-ol has an O–H group, so it forms hydrogen bonds between molecules; butanal (C=O, no O–H) has only dipole–dipole (and London) forces. Hydrogen bonds are stronger, so more energy is needed to separate butan-1-ol molecules → higher boiling point.

PBr3: (i) P with three P–Br bonds and one lone pair; each Br with three lone pairs. (ii) Trigonal pyramidal; angle <109.5° (≈101°; accept 100–109°). (iii) Polar: P–Br bonds are polar and the pyramidal shape is not symmetrical, so bond dipoles do not cancel – net dipole.

SF6: (i) S with six S–F bonds, no lone pairs on S; each F with three lone pairs (expanded octet). (ii) Octahedral; 90°. (iii) Non-polar: S–F bonds are polar but arranged symmetrically, so bond dipoles cancel – no net dipole.

Missing lone pairs on the terminal atoms are penalized once.

(i) σ bond: end-on (axial) overlap of orbitals, electron density concentrated between the two C nuclei. π bond: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, electron density above and below the internuclear axis.

(ii) HOOC–CH=CH–COOH: 11 σ and 3 π bonds.

(iii) The trans acid forms hydrogen bonds between molecules (intermolecular); in the cis isomer the two COOH groups are close together and form intramolecular H-bonds, so attractions between molecules are weaker → lower melting point for cis.

(iv) In the cis isomer the two COOH groups are on the same side and close together, so on heating they can eliminate water to form the cyclic anhydride; in trans they are too far apart.
O of the –OH group: sp3; O of C=O: sp2. Both oxygens must be identified.

(i) Aldehyde, –CHO (excess alcohol + distilling off removes it before further oxidation).

(ii) Increasing boiling point: Z < X < Y.
Z (aldehyde) cannot hydrogen bond with itself – only London and dipole–dipole forces.
X (alcohol) and Y (acid) both form hydrogen bonds; Y forms more/stronger H-bonds (two H-bonding sites, forms dimers) and is more polar, so it is highest.

(i) H3Si–SiH3: each Si has three Si–H bonding pairs plus the Si–Si pair (no lone pairs).

(ii) 109.5°: four electron domains (bonding pairs) around Si repel equally and adopt a tetrahedral arrangement.

(iii) sp3.

(iv) C–H is more polar: larger electronegativity difference (C–H 0.4, Si–H 0.3).

(v) Both are non-polar: symmetrical molecules so the bond dipoles cancel.

(vi) Disilane has more electrons, so stronger London (dispersion) forces between molecules – larger instantaneous dipoles. ("Larger mass" alone is not accepted.)

XeF4: Xe with four Xe–F bonds and two lone pairs (six electron domains); each F with three lone pairs. Shape: square planar (lone pairs opposite each other); angle 90°.

NO3−: N with one N=O double bond and two N–O single bonds, the single-bonded O atoms carrying the negative charges (brackets with 1− overall), all O lone pairs shown. Shape: trigonal planar; angle 120°.

(i) Mixing of atomic orbitals to form new, identical hybrid orbitals.

(ii) [3 max] C in methane is sp3. Ground state 1s22s22p2; one 2s electron is promoted (2s12p3); the 2s and three 2p orbitals mix to form four identical sp3 hybrid orbitals, which repel each other equally to point to the corners of a tetrahedron (109.5°).

(iii) Diamond: sp3. Graphite: sp2. In graphite each C uses three electrons in σ bonds; the fourth (in an unhybridized p orbital) is delocalized across the layer and can move, so graphite conducts.

Br2 is non-polar, so it has only London (dispersion) forces. ICl is polar (I and Cl differ in electronegativity), so it has dipole–dipole forces as well as London forces. With similar molar masses the London forces are similar, so the extra, stronger dipole–dipole attraction gives ICl the higher boiling point. Both IMF names are needed.

ICl3: I with three I–Cl bonds and two lone pairs (5 electron domains); each Cl with three lone pairs. Shape: T-shaped (lone pairs in equatorial positions).

[ICl2]−: I with two I–Cl bonds and three lone pairs; each Cl with three lone pairs; square brackets and 1− charge shown. Shape: linear (three lone pairs equatorial).

(i) P: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p3.

(ii) PCl3: P with three P–Cl bonds and one lone pair. PCl5: P with five P–Cl bonds and no lone pair (expanded octet). Each Cl has three lone pairs.

(iii) PCl3: trigonal pyramidal, about 107° (99–108° accepted). PCl5: trigonal bipyramidal, 90° and 120°.

(iv) sp3 (four electron domains).

(v) PCl5 has the higher melting point. It has more electrons (greater mass), so its London (dispersion) forces are stronger. Saying PCl3 is higher because it is polar scores only 1.

(vi) PCl5(s) + 4H2O(l) → H3PO4(aq) + 5HCl(aq). It hydrolyses to give an acidic solution.

• The p orbitals of the π bond overlap with a p orbital holding a lone pair on the other O atom, so the π electrons spread over all three atoms.
  • The π electrons are not localized between two atoms; two resonance structures can be drawn (O=O–O ↔ O–O=O).
  • Fact 1: both O–O bonds have the same length, between a single and a double bond.
  • Fact 2: both bonds have the same bond energy (bond order 1.5).
London (dispersion) forces and dipole–dipole forces. HI is polar, but H is not bonded to N, O or F, so there is no hydrogen bonding.

(i) (CH3)2NH. It has an N–H bond and a lone pair on the electronegative N, so it can form H-bonds with water (N–H···O and O–H···N). CH4 has no H bonded to N, O or F and no lone pair.

(ii) Draw a dashed line from the H of water's O–H to the lone pair on the N of (CH3)2NH, and/or from the N–H to a lone pair on the O of water.

(iii) N-methylmethanamine (dimethylamine).

(i) POCl3: P bonded to O (P=O, or P–O with formal charges) and to three Cl; no lone pair on P. Shape: tetrahedral. PCl3: three P–Cl bonds and one lone pair on P. Shape: trigonal pyramidal. Show the lone pairs on Cl and O.

(ii) The Cl–P–Cl angle is about 100° (100 to <109°). There are four electron domains (tetrahedral arrangement), but one is a lone pair, which repels more strongly than bonding pairs and squeezes the angle below 109.5°.

(iii) PCl3(l) + 3H2O(l) → H3PO3(aq) + 3HCl(aq)

(i) P with five P–Cl single bonds and no lone pair on P; each Cl has three lone pairs.

(ii) Trigonal bipyramidal.

(iii) 90°, 120° and 180°.

(iv) Isomers of PCl3Br2:

  • Both Br axial, all three Cl equatorial: non-polar, because the dipoles cancel.
  • Both Br equatorial, two Cl axial and one Cl equatorial: polar.
  • One Br axial and one equatorial: polar.
Carbon 1: sp2 (part of the C=C, three electron domains). Carbon 2: sp3 (four single bonds, tetrahedral).

Delocalization: the π electrons are shared over more than two nuclei; here the π bond (overlapping p orbitals) extends over N and all three O atoms.

Effect: all three N–O bonds have the same length and strength (bond order 1⅓), the charge is spread equally over the O atoms, and the ion is more stable (lower energy).
The N–N bond in trinitramide is longer (0.145 nm) than in N2 (0.110 nm), because trinitramide has a single N–N bond while N2 has a triple bond.

N–N–N angle ≈ 107° (106–108°, or <109° accepted). Any two reasons:

  • The central N has four electron domains, arranged tetrahedrally.
  • One of them is a lone pair, so the molecule is trigonal pyramidal.
  • The lone pair repels more than bonding pairs, squeezing the angle below 109.5°.
The molecule is polar. It is pyramidal, so the polar bond dipoles do not cancel and there is a net dipole moment. "Unsymmetrical" alone is not enough.

(i) In CO2, C is sp hybridized and each C=O bond is one σ + one π bond. In SiO2, Si is sp3 hybridized and each Si–O bond is a single σ bond only (giant tetrahedral network).

(ii) Si has four bonding domains, so the O atoms are arranged tetrahedrally around Si. In XeO2 (network), Xe has four bonding domains plus two lone pairs (six domains, octahedral). The lone pairs sit opposite each other, so the O atoms are square planar around Xe.
2-Methylbutan-2-ol has an –OH (hydroxyl) group, so it can form hydrogen bonds with water. The alkene is non-polar and cannot hydrogen-bond, so it is much less soluble.

(i) H2SO4(aq) + MgCO3(s) → MgSO4(aq) + CO2(g) + H2O(l). (Do not give H2CO3 as a product.)

(ii) Lewis structure: C in the centre with one C=O and two C–O single bonds; the double-bonded O has 2 lone pairs, each single-bonded O has 3 lone pairs; whole ion in square brackets with charge 2−. Shape: trigonal planar; O–C–O angle 120° (three electron domains, no lone pairs on C).

(iii) The π electrons are delocalized over all three C–O bonds (spread over more than two nuclei), so the charge is shared equally over the three O atoms and each bond is identical (bond order 1⅓).

(iv) sp2 (three σ bonds, one unhybridized p orbital forms the π system).

(i) HF has hydrogen bonding between molecules (H bonded to very electronegative F), which is much stronger than the forces in the other hydrogen halides.

(ii) From HCl to HI the London (dispersion) forces get stronger, because the number of electrons/size/molar mass of the molecule increases, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules.

(i) Hexane has a lower boiling point and enthalpy of vaporization, and a higher vapour pressure than pentan-1-ol.

(ii) Hexane is non-polar with only London (dispersion) forces – weaker intermolecular forces. Pentan-1-ol has hydrogen bonding between its molecules (–OH group), so more energy is needed to separate them and fewer escape into the vapour.

p2.key: Ethyl ethanoate (the ester). It has no O–H group, so it can form only weak hydrogen bonds with water (as an acceptor) and its hydrocarbon parts are relatively large, so it does not mix well with water.
O=O–O: central O has one lone pair, a double bond to one O (which has 2 lone pairs) and a single bond to the other O (which has 3 lone pairs). Formal charges/dative arrow not required.
Shape: bent (V-shaped) – three electron domains around the central O, one a lone pair. Bond angle: about 117° (115–119°; slightly less than 120° because the lone pair repels more).
sp2 (three electron domains).
